passages.t: Seeking by night, and the one she loves found
passages.happening:
‘On my bed at night I sought the one I love; I sought him, but did not find him’ (verse 1). She rises and goes through the streets and squares of the city, looking for him, and does not find him (verse 2).

She meets the watchmen on their rounds and asks whether they have seen the one she loves (verse 3). Just past them, she finds him. She holds him and will not let him go until she has brought him to her mother's house (verse 4).

And again the charge: “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 2 ended with the lovers belonging to each other. Chapter 3 opens with his absence. This is the first of two night searches in the Song (compare 5:2-8), and it shows love's other side: longing, anxiety and the fear of loss. It begins on a bed at night, and many readers take it as a dream or a vivid imagining of loss.

The phrase ‘the one I love’ is, in Hebrew, the one whom her soul loves, and it comes four times in these verses, with the verbs to seek and to find.

City watchmen patrolled the streets and walls at night against thieves and enemies. A woman alone in the streets after dark would draw attention and could be in danger.

Israelite households were usually named after the father, but the phrase mother's house appears in a few places linked with love and marriage, as when Rebekah runs to her mother's household (Genesis 24:28). Here it suggests a safe and close place, among her own family.
passages.later: Rebekah, after meeting Abraham's servant, ‘ran and told her mother’s household about these things’ (Genesis 24:28). And Naomi said to her daughters-in-law, ‘Go back, each of you to your mother’s home’ (Ruth 1:8).
passages.asks: She sought the one she loved and would not stop until she found him. Ask what you are seeking that much. And ask whether, in the nights of absence or fear, you have kept on looking for God, who promises to be found.

passages.t: A royal procession on the wedding day
passages.happening:
‘Who is this coming up from the wilderness like a column of smoke, scented with myrrh and frankincense from all the spices of the merchant?’ (verse 6).

‘Behold, it is Solomon’s carriage, escorted by sixty of the mightiest men of Israel’ (verse 7), each with his sword ready against the terrors of the night (verse 8). ‘King Solomon has made his carriage out of the timber of Lebanon’ (verse 9), with posts of silver, a base of gold and a seat of purple, its inside lovingly made by the daughters of Jerusalem (verse 10).

‘Come out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze at King Solomon, wearing the crown his mother bestowed on the day of his wedding’ (verse 11), the day of his heart's joy.
passages.hearers:
Many readers take this procession as the start of the Song's central section (3:6 to 5:1), where a wedding and its celebration are pictured.

Weddings in Israel often involved a procession, the groom and his friends coming to bring the bride home, or the bride being brought to the groom, with music and celebration. Myrrh and frankincense were costly imported resins used in worship and as perfume. The column of smoke may be incense, or the dust raised by the travelers.

The word for carriage, appiryon, appears only here in the Bible and may describe a palanquin, a covered litter carried on poles. Solomon's cedar came from Lebanon through his alliance with Hiram king of Tyre, and the sixty mighty men recall the elite warriors of David's time.

The crown from his mother would recall Bathsheba, who secured Solomon's throne, though the Old Testament records no ceremony in which she crowned him.
passages.later: A royal wedding psalm describes the same splendor: ‘All glorious is the princess in her chamber; her gown is embroidered with gold’ (Psalm 45:13). And the cedar of Lebanon came by treaty: ‘So Hiram provided Solomon with all the cedar and cypress timber he wanted’ (1 Kings 5:10).
passages.hard:
Is the man in the Song King Solomon, and how does that fit with Solomon's many wives?

Readers answer this in several ways.

Some take Solomon as the male lover throughout, and the Song as a celebration of one of his marriages, perhaps early in his reign, before his many foreign marriages led him astray (1 Kings 11:1-8). Others, following a view first proposed in the eighteenth century and made popular in the nineteenth, see three main characters: the woman, her shepherd lover, and Solomon, who tries to win her for his household while she stays faithful to the shepherd. A third view, common today, reads Solomon as a literary figure: the lovers picture each other as king and queen, just as they picture each other as shepherd and shepherdess, and the royal procession is how a wedding feels to those in love.

The Song's closing verses (8:11-12) seem to set Solomon's wealth beside the woman's freely given love, which supports the view that Solomon is not simply the hero. The text does not settle the question, and each view has thoughtful defenders. What is clear is that the Song celebrates a love that is faithful and given to one person alone, whatever Solomon's own record.
passages.asks: The Song pictures a wedding as a day of the heart's joy. If you are married, ask what you remember of that day's joy, and how you could honor it now. And whoever you are, ask how you can celebrate the faithful love you see in others.
